Barbara the Great Martyr

Icons

St. Barbara the Great Martyr

Barbara of Heliopolis

What is depictedHistory and traditionPublished explanationSources

The nineteenth-century Kastoria icon presents Barbara as a young crowned martyr. The image comes from the named Saint Barbara Church.

[1] Displayed work;file-level title,description,date and visual identification

What is depicted

Barbara wears richly patterned garments and holds a cross. The painted figure survives within a larger church setting rather than an invented new portrait. The file’s date and location describe this particular Kastoria depiction; they are not treated as the date or place of her martyrdom.

[1] Displayed work;file-level title,description,date and visual identification

History and tradition

The source identifies a nineteenth-century icon at Saint Barbara Church in Kastoria. The historical reference passage below preserves a received account of Dioscorus, the tower and the three windows. Its author’s distinction between later narrative and early evidence remains part of the reading’s bibliographic context.

[1] Displayed work;file-level title,description,date and visual identification

Published explanation

… According to these narratives, which are essentially the same, Barbara was the daughter of a rich heathen named Dioscorus. She was carefully guarded by her father who kept her shut up in a tower in order to preserve her from the outside world. An offer of marriage which was received through him she rejected. Before going on a journey her father commanded that a bath-house be erected for her use near her dwelling, and during his absence Barbara had three windows put in it, as a symbol of the Holy Trinity, instead of the two originally intended. …

Johann Peter Kirsch’s1907 Catholic Encyclopedia article attributes this story to later martyrdom narratives. It is not presented as a contemporary trial transcript.

[2] Article first paragraph,traditional narrative

… When her father returned she acknowledged herself to be a Christian; upon this she was ill-treated by him and dragged before the prefect of the province, Martinianus, who had her cruelly tortured and finally condemned her to death by beheading. The father himself carried out the death-sentence, but in punishment for this he was struck by lightning on the way home and his body consumed. Another Christian named Juliana suffered the death of a martyr along with Barbara. …

The same identified historical reference account;its source-critical setting is retained.

[2] Article first paragraph,confession and execution
